questions.q: What does the article call the greatest proof of the existence of God?
options: The size of the universe
Not quite. The article says: The existence of man himself – a conscious being who thinks, wills and acts.
The age of the earth
Not quite. The article says: The existence of man himself – a conscious being who thinks, wills and acts.
The existence of man himself – a conscious being who thinks, wills and acts
Yes. To accept one’s own existence is to have grounds for accepting God’s.
The testimony of ancient books
Not quite. The article says: The existence of man himself – a conscious being who thinks, wills and acts.
questions.rationale: “The greatest proof of the existence of God is the existence of man himself.”

questions.q: Why does the article call wasting time “a dual error”?
options: It is both a sin and a crime
Not quite. The article says: One wastes other people’s time along with one’s own.
One wastes other people’s time along with one’s own
Right. Punctuality is a form of goodwill to others.
It happens both morning and evening
Not quite. The article says: One wastes other people’s time along with one’s own.
It harms both body and mind
Not quite. The article says: One wastes other people’s time along with one’s own.
questions.rationale: “When you waste time, it is no simple matter, but it is a dual error. It means you are wasting the time of others along with your time.”

questions.q: “Speak to them in such terms as will address their minds” (4:63). How does the article apply this to today’s young people?
options: They should be left to find their own way
Not quite. The article says: Faith should be explained to them with reasons, not handed over as a list of dos and don’ts.
They should be given fewer responsibilities
Not quite. The article says: Faith should be explained to them with reasons, not handed over as a list of dos and don’ts.
Faith should be explained to them with reasons, not handed over as a list of dos and don’ts
Well read. This is the Age of Reason.
They should be addressed in a louder voice
Not quite. The article says: Faith should be explained to them with reasons, not handed over as a list of dos and don’ts.
questions.rationale: “One must not employ the method of ‘dos and don’ts’. Instead, religious beliefs should be presented in the light of rational arguments.”

questions.q: What does the article give as the condition for clarity in speech or writing?
options: Clear thinking beforehand – knowing what is relevant to the subject and what is not
Yes. Clear words follow clear thought.
Long experience of public speaking
Not quite. The article says: Clear thinking beforehand – knowing what is relevant to the subject and what is not.
A pleasing voice
Not quite. The article says: Clear thinking beforehand – knowing what is relevant to the subject and what is not.
A large vocabulary
Not quite. The article says: Clear thinking beforehand – knowing what is relevant to the subject and what is not.
questions.rationale: “The condition is that the speaker or writer should know the difference between relevant and irrelevant. He should have developed the quality of clarity in his thought before starting to speak or write.”

questions.article: Through the Eyes of the Intellect
questions.q: A poor widow wanted her son to learn a trade, but his teacher foresaw that learning would raise him high. Years later, at the Caliph’s table, what made the son laugh?
options: He was served the very delicacy his teacher had once said his knowledge would earn him
Correct. The teacher had seen with “the eyes of his intellect.”
He recognised his old teacher among the guests
Not quite. The article says: He was served the very delicacy his teacher had once said his knowledge would earn him.
The Caliph told a joke about washermen
Not quite. The article says: He was served the very delicacy his teacher had once said his knowledge would earn him.
He remembered that he had forgotten his mother
Not quite. The article says: He was served the very delicacy his teacher had once said his knowledge would earn him.
questions.rationale: “Imam Abu Hanifa said to my mother, ‘The knowledge he is acquiring will earn him pistachio faloodah’… One day, I was offered pistachio porridge.”

questions.article: Through the Eyes of the Intellect
questions.q: How, according to the article, does one develop “the eye of the intellect”?
options: By rising above surface appearances to look for the facts that lie behind them
Right. Like turning from what is near to see what is far.
By resting the physical eyes
Not quite. The article says: By rising above surface appearances to look for the facts that lie behind them.
By trusting first impressions
Not quite. The article says: By rising above surface appearances to look for the facts that lie behind them.
By reading faster
Not quite. The article says: By rising above surface appearances to look for the facts that lie behind them.
questions.rationale: “To develop this eye, a person needs to rise above the superficial observation. The facts lie behind the visible phenomena.”

questions.q: Einstein was slow to speak, was once expelled from school and failed an entrance examination. What does the article draw from his life?
options: Genius shows itself in infancy
Not quite. The article says: Greatness does not need a brilliant start; it can be reached from ordinary beginnings by sustained effort.
Greatness does not need a brilliant start; it can be reached from ordinary beginnings by sustained effort
Yes. Difficulty calls out hidden ability.
Schools are of little use
Not quite. The article says: Greatness does not need a brilliant start; it can be reached from ordinary beginnings by sustained effort.
Late talkers become scientists
Not quite. The article says: Greatness does not need a brilliant start; it can be reached from ordinary beginnings by sustained effort.
questions.rationale: “To achieve greatness, it is not necessary to be born great. A man can rise to greatness from the most obscure of beginnings, provided he is willing to strive for it.”

questions.q: Which observation of Sir Francis Bacon does the article quote on adversity?
options: “Adversity is the end of ambition”
Not quite. The article says: “Prosperity doth best discover vice, but adversity doth best discover virtue”.
“Prosperity doth best discover vice, but adversity doth best discover virtue”
Well read. Hardship brings out the best.
“Adversity makes strange bedfellows”
Not quite. The article says: “Prosperity doth best discover vice, but adversity doth best discover virtue”.
“Prosperity is the mother of invention”
Not quite. The article says: “Prosperity doth best discover vice, but adversity doth best discover virtue”.
questions.rationale: “Prosperity doth best discover vice, but adversity doth best discover virtue.”

questions.q: On his pilgrimage the Prophet began the walk between the two hills at Safa, saying, “I am starting where God started.” What does the article see in this?
options: A preference for simplicity – following the order in the Quran spared people from remembering two different sequences
Well reasoned. Free of needless complication.
A wish to finish the rite quickly
Not quite. The article says: A preference for simplicity – following the order in the Quran spared people from remembering two different sequences.
A choice made at random
Not quite. The article says: A preference for simplicity – following the order in the Quran spared people from remembering two different sequences.
A custom older than the Quran
Not quite. The article says: A preference for simplicity – following the order in the Quran spared people from remembering two different sequences.
questions.rationale: “The Prophet adopted the same sequence in pilgrimage as had been followed in the Quran, thus saving people the trouble of remembering two different orders. Simplicity is a factor essential to the spirit of Islam.”

questions.q: The reviewer praises the book but differs from it on one point – how man should regard nature. What view does the reviewer prefer?
options: Nature should be left entirely untouched
Not quite. The article says: Nature is a gift from God to be respected and cared for by man as its trustee, not merely conquered and exploited.
Nature is a gift from God to be respected and cared for by man as its trustee, not merely conquered and exploited
Exactly. Neither worshipped nor abused.
Nature has no value in itself
Not quite. The article says: Nature is a gift from God to be respected and cared for by man as its trustee, not merely conquered and exploited.
Nature should be worshipped
Not quite. The article says: Nature is a gift from God to be respected and cared for by man as its trustee, not merely conquered and exploited.
questions.rationale: “Nature is a gift from God, not a thing to be worshipped, but, still, something to be respected, to be taken good care of by man and to be wisely and kindly harnessed.”
